Keywords: There, The, Just

outputs.L1:
There is magic in decay—
a dance to be done
for the rotting, the maggot-strewn
piles of flesh that mount
upon the dung-ridden earth,
and the damp that gathers
and rusts and defiles.

There is a trace of this
in even the most zoetic soul—
the dancing child's arms,
flailing to an old ska song,
usher the day-old flies
away toward whatever rank
haven lies closest.

Just today
I was walking along the river
with my daughter in my backpack,
and I opened my email
on my phone, and Duffie
had sent me a poem
called "Compost." I read it
to my little girl and began
to explain before I was three
words in when Selma started
yelling, Daddy, Daddy, snake!
In the path lay a snake,
belly up and still nerve-twitching,
the ghost of some passing
bicycle or horse.

Pretty, Selma said.
Yes, I said. And beneath my yes,
another yes—the yes to my body,
just beginning to show signs
of slackening—and another, my grasping
in the dark for affirming flesh
that in turn says yes, yes,
let us rot together, but not until
we have drained what sap
remains in these trees.

And I wake in the morning
and think of the coroner
calling to ask what color
my father's eyes were,
and I asked, Why? Why can't
you simply look—and the coroner,
matter-of-factly, says, Decay.

Do you want some eggs, my love?
I have a new way of preparing them.
And look, look outside—I think this weather
stands a chance of holding.
outputs.L2:
Beauty hides within things that fall apart.

There's a rhythm meant for what's decaying,
for the worm-covered heaps
of flesh that gather
on soil thick with manure,
where moisture pools
and corrodes and stains.

A trace of this exists
in even the most vibrant, living spirit—
the child who dances, arms
thrashing to some vintage ska tune,
waving off flies a day old
toward the nearest
foul-smelling place.

This very morning
I strolled beside the river,
my daughter riding in my pack,
and checked my email
on my phone. Duffie
had sent along a poem
titled "Compost." I read it
aloud to my small child and began
to describe it, but before I'd said
even three words, Selma began
shouting, Daddy, Daddy, snake!
There on the trail lay a snake,
overturned and twitching still,
haunted by some passing
bicycle or horse.

Pretty, said Selma.
Yes, I agreed. And beneath that yes
lay another yes, the yes I give my body,
which is only starting to reveal
its loosening, and another yes—
my reaching through darkness
toward flesh that affirms,
that answers back yes, yes,
let's decay together, though not before
we've drawn out whatever sap
remains within these trees.

Then I wake come morning
and remember the coroner
phoning to ask the color
of my father's eyes,
and I said, Why? Why not
simply look—and the coroner,
plainly, replied, Decay.

Would you like some eggs, my love?
I've discovered a fresh way to cook them.
And look, look outdoors—I believe this weather
just might last.
outputs.L3:
# Finding Beauty in Decay

The poem discovers an unexpected beauty and magic within decay, rot, and decomposition, refusing to view these processes as purely negative or frightening. Instead of recoiling from the natural breakdown of living things, the poem embraces decomposition as a source of wonder—a transformation that carries its own strange enchantment. This perspective invites readers to reconsider their instinctive aversion to endings and to find something worthy of contemplation in what most would rather ignore.

This connection to decay is not limited to the obviously lifeless. Even the most vibrant and animated beings—like a child caught in the joy of dancing—carry within them an element of this link to death and dissolution. Life and decay are not opposites but intimately bound together, present even in moments of exuberant vitality. The dancing child, so full of energy and light, still participates in the same cycle that governs all living things.

This theme becomes concrete during a walk the speaker takes with his daughter, Selma. Together they come upon a dead snake lying in their path, and in her innocence, Selma calls it "pretty." Her childlike response captures the poem's central insight perfectly: without the learned fear or revulsion that adults bring to death, she sees only beauty. Her simple observation blends the categories of the beautiful and the dead, collapsing the distance that we usually maintain between them.

From this encounter, the speaker turns inward to reflect on his own aging body and his longing for intimate connection with another person. He frames love and mortality not as separate experiences but as deeply intertwined—imagining closeness with a partner as a kind of "rotting together." In this vision, to love someone is to share in the slow process of decline, to decompose alongside them. Intimacy and decay become inseparable, two aspects of the same tender, mortal experience.

Finally, a memory rises to the surface: a coroner once asked the speaker about his deceased father's eye color, explaining that the question was necessary because of "decay." The speaker sets this stark, unsettling recollection against the ordinary textures of domestic life—the simple acts of making eggs for breakfast, of noticing the weather outside. In this juxtaposition, the poem reveals how death and decay are woven quietly into the fabric of everyday existence, coexisting with the mundane routines that carry us through our days.
outputs.L4:
# Decay and Vitality: A Reading

This poem takes as its central preoccupation the intertwined realities of decay and mortality, but it approaches these vast subjects not through abstraction or philosophical argument, but through a series of small, intimate, deeply personal moments that accumulate into something like a meditation. The poet weaves together disparate threads of experience, allowing each to illuminate the others, until the reader comes to understand that decay is not the enemy of life but its constant companion.

The first thread is a walk the poet takes with a daughter. This is an image of tenderness and continuity—the older generation accompanying the younger, life passing forward through time. Yet even this scene of familial love is not sheltered from the presence of death. On the path they encounter a dead snake, its body already given over to the processes of decomposition. The snake becomes a quiet emblem of the way mortality intrudes upon even our gentlest moments, lying directly in the path of the living.

Alongside these lived experiences, the poet introduces a self-referential element: a poem titled "Compost." Compost is, of course, the perfect governing metaphor for the entire work. It names the process by which what has died and rotted becomes the very ground of new growth—the decay that feeds vitality, the breakdown that makes creation possible. By naming a poem within the poem, the writer signals that art itself participates in this cycle, transforming loss and rot into something nourishing.

Then comes the most piercing and specific moment: a coroner's call concerning the poet's deceased father, and specifically a question or observation about the dead man's eyes. Here mortality becomes fully personal and unavoidable. The eyes—traditionally the windows of the soul, the organs of vision and connection—are now the subject of a clinical, bureaucratic inquiry after death. This detail grounds the poem's larger themes in raw grief and the strange indignities that accompany the death of someone we love.

What makes the poem remarkable is that it refuses to let these encounters with death collapse into despair. Instead, through their careful interweaving, the poem arrives at a hard-won affirmation. It reveals that decay is inseparable from vitality and from love—that the same processes which break the body down are the ones that renew the world, that make room for the daughter's future, that turn death into compost for life. 

In the end, the poem offers a bodily "yes"—an affirmation not merely intellectual but visceral, rooted in the flesh that will one day rot and in the flesh that presently loves and walks and touches. It says yes to intimacy, yes to the ongoing life shared with a daughter, yes to the natural cycle of rotting and renewal. Even in the shadow of a father's death and a snake's carcass, even with the coroner's voice still echoing, the poet chooses to embrace the whole of existence: not life purified of death, but life inextricable from it, whole and continuous and, finally, worthy of assent.

# There, The, Just: The Quiet Power of Small Words

Some of the most powerful words in the English language are also the smallest. Take three simple examples: **There**, **The**, and **Just**. At first glance, they seem unremarkable—the kind of words we skip over without a second thought. Yet each one carries surprising weight in how we communicate.

## There

**There** is a word of presence and possibility. It points us toward a place, an idea, or a fact of existence. When we say "There is hope," we affirm that something real exists. When we say "Look over there," we direct someone's attention beyond themselves. *There* opens up space—it tells us that the world extends outward, that something waits just beyond where we stand.

## The

**The** may be the most common word in English, and for good reason. It is the great identifier, the word that turns something general into something specific. "A book" could be any book, but "the book" is *that* particular one we both know. With a single syllable, **the** creates focus, shared understanding, and importance. It quietly shapes nearly every sentence we speak.

## Just

**Just** wears many hats. It can mean fairness—"a just decision"—reminding us of morality and balance. It can soften a request—"just a moment, please"—or emphasize the exact truth of something—"that's just perfect." In its smallness, **just** carries both precision and grace, capturing everything from patience to justice.

## Conclusion

**There** shows us what exists. **The** helps us name it clearly. **Just** reminds us to see it fairly and precisely. Together, these humble words prove that meaning does not depend on length. Sometimes the smallest words do the greatest work—we just have to notice them.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free verse poem about finding beauty in decay and mortality, weaving together everyday moments with a partner and child.
counterfactuals.output:
# What Remains

The banana on the counter
has gone soft, brown-freckled,
and my daughter presses her thumb
into its yielding skin, delighted—
*look, it's melting*—
and I don't say *rotting*,
because she has found the sweetness
in the surrender.

You are graying at the temples.
I watched it happen slowly,
the way frost takes a window,
and I have come to love
this evidence of days,
these silver proofs
that you were here, and here, and here.

We are all becoming compost
for something.

Even this morning—
the light through the kitchen
already older than it looks,
having traveled minutes
just to touch the toast crumbs,
the dried ring of last night's wine,
the small chapped hand
reaching for another bite.

I used to fear the ending of things.
Now I fold the laundry warm,
still smelling of the three of us,
and I understand
that nothing lasts
is not a warning
but an invitation:

be here
in the softening fruit,
the fading afternoon,
the way our child
will not be small tomorrow,

be here
where everything
is briefly, unbearably
beautiful

because it goes.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a contemporary poem that begins with the line "There is magic in decay" and moves through images of rot, family life, and death.
counterfactuals.output:
# There Is Magic in Decay

There is magic in decay,
in the soft brown edges of the peach
left too long on the counter,
its sweetness deepening toward wine
before it turns to fur.

My mother knew this—
how she let the compost breathe
in its plastic bucket by the sink,
coffee grounds and eggshells,
the ends of things becoming
the beginnings of tomatoes.

We are all composting.
The children spill their milk
and it sours in the carpet's memory.
The father's beard goes gray
like moss claiming a stone.
Even love ferments—
grows stranger, richer,
harder to name.

I watched my grandmother's hands
grow spotted as old fruit,
the skin thinning to translucence
until you could nearly see
the light pass through her,
the way it passes through
a leaf in autumn
just before it lets go.

There is a mushroom
that only fruits from what has fallen,
that needs the death of the tree
to make its brief white bloom.
This is not sad.
This is the arithmetic of dirt,
the patient math
by which a body becomes a garden.

When my time comes,
let me be a peach forgotten
on some warm windowsill of earth.
Let me go soft.
Let me feed whatever
comes next hungry to the table—
and let them taste,
in whatever grows from me,
the sweetness I was ripening toward
all along.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem exploring how the awareness of death and physical decline coexists with love, desire, and ordinary domestic life.
counterfactuals.output:
**Inventory**

The dishes wait. I wash them anyway,
knowing my hands will one day stop their work,
knowing the water running down the drain
rehearses every leaving. Still—the plates
come clean. The evening settles like a cat.

You call from the other room about the milk,
whether we need it, and I answer *yes*
as if there were no last time coming for us,
as if the word *tomorrow* were a floor
and not a rope stretched over open air.

Here is the strange arithmetic of days:
that I can want you—want the warm particular
weight of you against me in the dark—
while somewhere in my chest a clock is spending
its exact allotment, coin by coin.

The body is a house we're asked to leave
without a forwarding address. And yet
we hang the pictures. Yet we paint the walls.
Yet I reach for you across the narrowing years
and find you reaching back, both of us aware

that this is how it ends: not with a flourish
but with a folded towel, a lifted glass,
a hand laid on a shoulder in the kitchen.
The dishes done. The lamp still on. The two of us
practicing forever in the only tense we have.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: I want a literary poem that connects a dead snake on a path, a coroner's phone call, and an intimate morning scene—all meditating on decay and vitality.
counterfactuals.output:
**Three Notifications of the Living**

On the path this morning, a snake laid out
like a discarded belt, its body a sentence
the heat had finished writing. Already
the ants had come to read it, to translate
the muscle back to earth's first language.
I stepped around it the way we step
around all evidence—carefully, and with a kind
of gratitude that isn't ours to feel.

The coroner called while I was making coffee.
Not for me. For my father, dead a week,
some final form, some box that wanted checking.
*And how was the deceased found?* she asked,
her voice so kind it made the kitchen tilt.
I said *at rest,* though he was not.
I said *peacefully,* the way we lie
to keep the living from becoming stone.

But you were still asleep when I came back to bed,
your shoulder rising, falling, rising—
that small tide the body keeps against
the argument of endings. I put my mouth
against your spine and counted vertebrae,
each one a knuckle in the fist that holds us
here, and warm, and briefly. You turned.
You said my name as if it were a country
you had visited in dreams and meant to stay.

Everything is leaving. The snake unspools
its heat into the grass. My father's name
goes cold inside a file. And yet your breath
was on my throat like something being born,
and the coffee cooled, and the ants worked on,
and the whole earth ate its dead to make
the living lush—this is the only prayer
I know: to lie down in the wreck of it
and still reach out. To still, somehow, reach out.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem in the style of a modern confessional poet about a father walking with his daughter, receiving a poem called "Compost," and reflecting on his own aging body and his father's death.
counterfactuals.output:
**Compost**

My daughter hands me a poem
she wrote in the car, the paper soft
already from her hands, and calls it *Compost*—
how the dead things feed the living,
she explains, not looking up,
the way peels and eggshells and the brown
collapsing lettuce become, in the dark
of the bin, a black richness
you can hold. She is nine.
She does not know she has just described
my body to me on a Tuesday.

We are walking to the end of the road
where the fields begin, and I feel
the small machine of my knee
click like a latch, feel the way
the skin on the back of my hand
has begun to slacken and pleat,
the same hand, the same slackening
I held in the hospital, my father's,
the last week, when his fingers
were already going that color,
the loosening, the letting-go
the earth practices on all of us slowly
before it makes it quick.

He fed me. That is the ugly truth
the poem in my pocket keeps insisting.
Everything I am was pulled up
out of the ruin of him—
his temper, his blue eyes,
the way I clear my throat
before I say a hard thing.
Now I am the layer on top,
and beneath me, warm and working,
my girl is climbing the split-rail fence,
her whole body a green shoot,
her laughter the steam that rises
off the pile in cold weather,
proof of a heat I can't see.

I want to tell her: yes, and also
one day these hands, this voice
you know so well you don't hear it—
I want to tell her nothing.
I take the poem out and read it again
so she'll see me reading it,
so she'll know that I received it,
that the message got through,
that the man walking beside her
understood exactly what he was:
food, love, dirt, the good dark
she will one day stand on
and call by his first name.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
